name: Dr. Clement Ketterly
languages: German (two semesters, for the medical journals)
equipment: Heavy coat: a dark blue chesterfield from a Charleston tailor, entirely wrong for a coal camp
Scalpel, one of a set of six in a roll in his doctor's bag
Doctor's bag: stethoscope, sphygmomanometer, a hypodermic and morphine, iodine, carbolic, sutures, splints, bandages, a clinical thermometer and a copy of a pocket formulary
His contract with the Ottway Smokeless Coal Company: company physician at $250 a month, paid out of the dollar a month the company stops from every miner's wages for 'doctor'
A letter of introduction from his father to Superintendent Elwood Bledsoe, which calls him 'my boy, who will be no trouble'

A copy of the public transcript of the Selden County coroner's inquest into the Ottway No. 3 explosion of 14 October 1919, taken from his father's office shelf without asking, because he was curious about the place
A leather notebook in which he records every patient: name, check number, complaint and what he did
An electric flashlight, new, with two spare batteries
features: The Family Name (Old Family origin: in Charleston and among the propertied and professional of the state he is received, offered a chair and told things a stranger is not; advantage on Persuasion with them; once per scenario, an introduction or a meeting with someone of standing without a check; the name also comes with its debts, and in Ottway it means the company's lawyers)

Steady Hands (Physician, using Intelligence: as an action with his doctor's bag, a creature he touches spends up to 2 Hit Dice as on a short rest and regains 3 extra hit points; it also stabilizes the dying and ends Bleeding; 4 uses per long rest. Treat Shock: during a short rest, everyone resting with him loses 1 extra Dread, even at Dread 4 or more)

Diagnosis (Physician: as a bonus action, learns a creature's current and maximum hit points, its conditions and roughly what its Dread is; 10 minutes with a body gives cause and time of death without a check, and whether anything is wrong with it in a way medicine cannot account for; one more detail on a DC 12 Medicine check)

Clinical Detachment (Physician, 2nd level: advantage on fear checks against wounds, bodies, blood and the ordinary dead, and he can examine anything a fear check would cost him Dread to see with no fear check at all, if he does nothing else for that minute)

Practice: Coroner (Physician, 3rd level: he can request any death record, autopsy report or inquest file in Selden County, and as the company physician he is also, by an old county arrangement, a deputy coroner; examining any victim of a creature gives one clue toward one of its rules)

Library Privileges (Student background: a year out of Jefferson Medical College in Philadelphia and his internship; he can get into any academic or medical library and many private ones, and people explain things to him more patiently than to anyone else)

personality.traits: I am polite to everyone and I apologise to people I examine. I believe there is a reason for everything and it can usually be found in a textbook. I have never been hungry and I am beginning to understand that this is a fact about me.
personality.ideals: A doctor's first duty is to the patient in front of him, not to whoever pays him. I have said this at dinner in Charleston many times. Ottway is the first place I have had to find out whether I meant it.
personality.bonds: My father, Garrett Ketterly, of Ketterly & Bowyer, counsel to half the coal companies in the state, whom I love and am starting to be afraid of. My patients, whose names I write down. Vesta Spradlin, from the moment she comes to my office.
personality.flaws: I trust people who speak the way I do. I want very much to be told that what I am seeing is not what it looks like, and the company is very good at telling me.

appearance: A tall, fair, soft-handed young man of twenty-seven with a long kind face, gold-rimmed spectacles, a carefully trimmed moustache he grew to look older, and good shoes that will not last a week in the camp. He stands very straight, as he was taught, and has begun, without noticing, to stoop when he goes into the miners' houses.
backstory: Clement Ketterly is the second son of Garrett Ketterly, the most successful coal lawyer in Charleston, and grew up in a house on the Kanawha with a cook, a car and a portrait of a great-grandfather who was in the legislature. He wanted to be a doctor from the age of nine, when the family doctor set his broken arm, and his father agreed on condition that he do it properly: Jefferson Medical College in Philadelphia and a hospital internship. When old Dr. Whitlock retired from the Ottway camp in February, his father's client, the Ottway Smokeless Coal Company, needed a physician, and his father thought a year in a coal camp would be good for him before he took a Charleston practice. He comes in on the same train as the others, with a contract, a letter to the superintendent, and the inquest transcript he took from his father's office shelf. He has read it twice on the train. It says thirteen men died instantly in the explosion and that the section was sealed against fire on 15 October 1919 'in accordance with accepted practice and with the concurrence of the District Mine Inspector'. On page forty, a seal-crew witness named Washington Burchett is asked whether he heard anything from behind the seal while he worked, and the transcript says: '(Witness did not answer.) Q: Let the record show the witness is excused.' Clement has not been able to stop thinking about that line.
